source.title: Scaling Reasoning Tokens via RL and Parallel Thinking: Evidence From Competitive Programming
source.authors: Qianfan Zhang; Tian-Yu Guo; Xuan-Di Ren; Jia-Le Chen; Ming Ding; Ran Xin; Xia Xiao

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether accuracy scales with reasoning-token budget in competitive programming, using RL and test-time inference rather than pretraining cross-entropy scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy against parameter count, training tokens, or pretraining compute; it does not test extrapolation from small pretraining runs, a compute-optimal parameter/token split, architecture-shape effects, or other modalities. Its own accuracy-versus-reasoning-token results bear on V6. The paper also discusses verification metrics, but those do not measure downstream accuracy scaling and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper cites pretraining scaling laws (Kaplan, Hoffmann) only as background. Its results concern competitive-programming accuracy against generated reasoning tokens. These come from RL checkpoints of one 36B model and from test-time verify/refine pipelines. No result varies parameters, pretraining tokens or pretraining compute, or measures pretraining loss. V6 is about downstream performance improving with model or pretraining scale or loss. Reasoning-token and test-time compute scaling is a related but different construct, so the findings go under fits_no_version rather than V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress several further points. A quadratic-attention compute wall limits RL length scaling. Sequential refinement beats parallel generation at every budget. End-to-end RL overtakes separate training at high budgets. The full 16×16 pipeline matches the RL model's oracle pass@16 at pass@1 and surpasses GPT-5-high. They call the log-linear trend an empirical regularity of their setup, not a universal law.
record.recipe_differences: Measures competitive-programming accuracy against RL-generated reasoning-token budgets and test-time compute, rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy against parameters, training tokens, or compute; does not fit or test the original pretraining scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed accuracy-token trajectory changes with randomized clipping and verification RL warmup. Test-time results differ between sequential refinement, parallel generation, their combination, and the training method (turn-grouped GRPO versus REINFORCE).

fits_no_version.finding: Across RL checkpoints of Seed-OSS-36B, AetherCode accuracy rises approximately linearly in log(average reasoning tokens). Randomized clipping steepens the slope and verification warmup raises the intercept. The no-warmup run plateaus near 0.33.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: During RL for reasoning, downstream accuracy scales log-linearly with average generated reasoning tokens, with recipe-dependent slope and intercept.

fits_no_version.finding: Test-time accuracy rises with the total token budget. Sequential refinement gives ~0.49 at 160K and plateaus at ~0.55 at ~500K. Parallel generation gives ~0.45 at 160K. Combining both reaches ~0.61 at 7.6M tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time reasoning compute (sequential and parallel) improves downstream accuracy roughly log-linearly until a method-specific plateau.

fits_no_version.finding: Oracle pass@k grows with the sampling budget. Generation RL reaches ~0.73 at pass@256 versus ~0.57–0.59 for SFT and verification RL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated-sampling coverage scales with the number of samples, and RL can raise the coverage ceiling.

record.problems: The experiments use proprietary training problems and one stated base model; the reported accuracy curves are largely not numerically tabulated, and no uncertainty intervals are reported. The authors explicitly caution that the RL log-linear trend is specific to their observed setup rather than a universal law.
record.rows_left_out: Verification-RL recall, precision, and accuracy measurements in Section 2.3 are verification metrics rather than downstream accuracy-versus-scale results. No other qualifying V6 numerical results were left out.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss, and no variation of parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small pretraining runs.
No loss power laws in other modalities or regimes. The RL accuracy-token trend is not a loss power law.
No downstream performance measured against model size, pretraining compute or pretraining loss. Only one base model is used.
No comparison of pretraining-law fits or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link is rejected. V6 concerns downstream predictability from model or pretraining scale or loss. This paper scales reasoning or test-time tokens for a single 36B model. Many rows are the study's own method comparisons (RC, warmup, GRPO vs REINFORCE, separate vs end-to-end training, verdict count) and would not be rows even under a matching version. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy or power-law fit in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of much larger pretraining runs from fits to small runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep over model parameter count and training-token count.
No comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests of power-law scaling in other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

Tests competitive-programming accuracy against reasoning-token budgets during RL and at test time; does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss or model parameter scale.
Does not compare pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices. It reports recipe-dependent changes to a different, accuracy-versus-reasoning-token trend.

rows.subject: Seed-OSS-36B-Base generation RL checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation accuracy across successive generation-RL checkpoints as average generated reasoning-token count increased.
rows.measure: Validation accuracy versus average reasoning tokens
rows.value: Approximately log-linear: accuracy increases linearly with the logarithm of average token count.
rows.note: The authors describe this as an empirical regularity of their setup, not a universal law; the plotted checkpoints are not numerically tabulated.
rows.check: Accuracy versus reasoning tokens across RL checkpoints of a single model. This is not downstream scaling with model or pretraining scale or loss.

rows.subject: Seed-OSS-36B-Base generation RL with randomized clipping
rows.operation_detail: Replaced the fixed response-length cap with a uniformly sampled cap, using a = 60000 and b = 90000.
rows.measure: Validation accuracy versus average reasoning tokens
rows.baseline: Baseline generation RL with a hard maximum token limit of 90000
rows.value: Randomized clipping produces a steeper log-linear trend and better accuracy at a fixed reasoning-token budget.
rows.note: The text states the direction of the effect; the plotted accuracy values are not tabulated.
rows.check: Compares the study's own randomized-clipping method with its baseline. It is an RL recipe effect, not claim scaling.

rows.subject: Seed-OSS-36B-Base generation RL without verification RL warmup
rows.operation_detail: Trained generation RL directly from the SFT initialization, without verification RL warmup.
rows.value: Approximately 0.33; the run plateaus at this level.
rows.note: The reported plateau qualifies the claim that accuracy keeps improving as reasoning-token length increases.
rows.check: Plateau of RL accuracy versus generation length. This is a reasoning-token construct, not model or pretraining scale.

rows.subject: Seed-OSS-36B-Base generation RL initialized from verification RL
rows.operation_detail: Applied verification RL warmup before generation RL.
rows.baseline: Approximately 0.33 for generation RL without verification warmup at approximately 70000 average tokens
rows.note: The warm-started run is reported as more accurate at a similar token count.
rows.check: Method comparison (verification RL warmup versus none) at matched tokens.

rows.subject: Seed-OSS-36B-Base generation RL initialized from verification RL
rows.operation_detail: Continued generation RL with an extended maximum context length.
rows.measure: AetherCode validation accuracy versus average reasoning tokens
rows.baseline: Original budget range with a 90000 maximum context length
rows.value: Continues improving beyond the original budget range while remaining consistent with the same overall trend.
rows.note: No additional numerical accuracy or token values are stated in the text for this extension.
rows.check: Context-length extension of RL. This is reasoning-token scaling, not model scale.

rows.subject: End-to-end RL checkpoint (turn-grouped GRPO)
rows.operation_detail: Increased sequential verify-refine rounds with one thread.
rows.baseline: Single generation from the end-to-end RL checkpoint: approximately 0.34 accuracy at approximately 60000 tokens
rows.note: Sequential refinement is reported to outperform parallel generation at every token budget.
rows.check: Test-time sequential refinement scaling. This is test-time compute, not model or pretraining scale.

rows.subject: End-to-end RL checkpoint (turn-grouped GRPO)
rows.operation_detail: Increased sequential verify-refine rounds with one thread.
rows.note: The stated plateau shows that sequential refinement does not continue improving indefinitely with more reasoning tokens.
rows.check: Test-time sequential plateau (~0.55 at ~500K tokens). This is a different construct.

rows.subject: End-to-end RL checkpoint (turn-grouped GRPO)
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of independent threads, with one generation round per thread.
rows.note: Parallel scaling is less token-efficient than sequential refinement at the reported matched budget.
rows.check: Parallel versus sequential comparison of the study's own pipeline variants.

rows.subject: End-to-end RL checkpoint (turn-grouped GRPO)
rows.operation_detail: Combined sequential verify-refine rounds with increasing numbers of threads.

conditions.value: 7.6 million tokens per problem on average

rows.baseline: Underlying RL model's oracle pass@16 is the stated comparison
rows.value: Approximately 0.61; reported to match the underlying RL model's oracle pass@16 and surpass GPT-5-high.
rows.note: The paper does not state a numeric value for the underlying model's oracle pass@16 in this passage.
rows.check: Full pipeline result (~0.61 at 7.6M tokens). This is the study's own method performance under test-time compute.

rows.subject: Separately trained generation and verification RL model
rows.stage_stated: Verification RL followed by generation RL
rows.baseline: End-to-end RL checkpoint: 0.34 at the comparison's approximately 65.5K-token starting point
rows.note: The separately trained model starts approximately 4 points higher than the end-to-end RL model.
rows.check: Compares separate training with end-to-end RL (the study's own methods). The value and baseline are the starting points of two methods.

rows.subject: End-to-end RL checkpoint (turn-grouped GRPO)

conditions.value: highest budgets shown, up to 5.12M on Figure 6

rows.baseline: Separately trained model: approximately 0.60 at the highest budgets
rows.note: The paper says the end-to-end model catches up by approximately 2M tokens and slightly exceeds the separate-training model at the highest budgets.
rows.check: Method comparison at the highest budgets (0.61 vs 0.60).

rows.subject: End-to-end RL checkpoint (REINFORCE with batch-level whitening)

conditions.value: highest budgets shown; REINFORCE evaluation truncated at N = 8 threads and M = 8 rounds

rows.baseline: End-to-end RL with turn-grouped GRPO: approximately 0.61 at the highest budgets
rows.note: The REINFORCE run was evaluated only over the truncated thread-and-round range.
rows.check: REINFORCE versus turn-grouped GRPO method comparison. The REINFORCE evaluation was truncated at N=8, M=8.

rows.subject: Early end-to-end RL checkpoint (turn-grouped GRPO)
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of verification verdict samples while holding refinement off.
rows.locator: Appendix A, Figure 7 and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper reports that increasing verdict samples improves accuracy modestly; the oracle pass@8 reference is approximately 0.54.
rows.check: Ablation of the number of verdicts (V=1) in the study's own pipeline.

rows.subject: Early end-to-end RL checkpoint (turn-grouped GRPO)
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of verification verdict samples while holding refinement off.
rows.locator: Appendix A, Figure 7 and accompanying text
rows.note: More verdict samples improve accuracy, but the reported result remains below oracle pass@8.
rows.check: Ablation of the number of verdicts (V=8) in the study's own pipeline.

rows.subject: SFT cold-start checkpoint
rows.operation_detail: Measured oracle pass@k as the number of sampled generations and token budget increased.
rows.locator: Appendix B, Figure 8 and accompanying text
rows.note: Reported as the low-k comparison with verification RL; this is an oracle sampling curve, not pretraining-loss scaling.
rows.check: Oracle pass@1 of the SFT checkpoint. This is a training-stage comparison, not scale.

rows.subject: Verification RL checkpoint
rows.operation_detail: Measured oracle pass@k as the number of sampled generations and token budget increased.
rows.locator: Appendix B, Figure 8 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors interpret this as improved per-sample quality after verification RL.
rows.check: Oracle pass@1 of the verification RL checkpoint compared with SFT. This is a training-stage comparison.

rows.subject: Verification RL checkpoint
rows.operation_detail: Measured oracle pass@k as the number of sampled generations and token budget increased.
rows.baseline: SFT cold start: approximately 0.57–0.59 at pass@256
rows.locator: Appendix B, Figure 8 and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper says verification RL and SFT converge at pass@256.
rows.check: Convergence at pass@256 across training stages. This bears on RL coverage, not on the scaling claim.

rows.subject: Generation RL checkpoint initialized from verification RL
rows.operation_detail: Measured oracle pass@k as the number of sampled generations and token budget increased.
rows.baseline: SFT cold start and verification RL: approximately 0.57–0.59 at pass@256
rows.locator: Appendix B, Figure 8 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors interpret the persistent gap at large k as expanded solution coverage.
rows.check: Generation RL pass@256 (~0.73) versus earlier stages. This is a training-stage comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: RL validation accuracy and combined test-time sequential-plus-parallel scaling on AetherCode
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy rises with reasoning-token budget in the reported RL trend and reaches approximately 0.61 at 7.6 million tokens in the combined pipeline (R1, R9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Baseline generation RL and sequential-only test-time refinement
reader_labels.reason: Baseline generation RL plateaus near 0.33, and sequential refinement reaches approximately 0.55 before plateauing; the trend is not unbounded (R3, R7).
